one_line_contribution: A bank-swap diagnostic (D_swap = acc(own bank) - acc(swapped bank)) that quantifies how much of a reflectively-optimized instruction's gain is bound to the particular experience bank it was optimized against, plus a cost-annotated head-to-head of five candidate fixes in which the load-bearing new contrast is optimization-time memory masking (p=0.5) versus the zero-cost deployment-time alternative of lowering injection top-k on an already co-adapted instruction (E2/P8).
closest_prior_work: Two threats, neither engaged adequately. (1) The RAG robustness-to-context-perturbation literature the proposal itself concedes (FiD-style stochastic document dropping; Yoran et al.-style training with irrelevant/randomized retrieved context) already establishes the general result that randomizing retrieved context during optimization buys robustness to changed retrieved context at deployment. The proposal moves this from weights to instruction text, which is a venue change, not a mechanism change, and makes P2 a low-surprise prediction. (2) More damaging for the *diagnostic*: overfitting of automatically-optimized prompts to the exact trainset/demonstration set they were searched against is well-documented in the MIPROv2/DSPy and APE/OPRO line (validation overfitting, demonstration-order and demonstration-identity sensitivity). The proposal's argument that MIPROv2 'freezes the demo set so there is no turnover' defends against priority on the *setting*, not on the *finding*: a reviewer will say P1 restates known prompt-search overfitting with a memory bank playing the role of the demo set. Separately, the research brief handed to the authors explicitly names ReasoningBank and '2026 successors' as the relevant memory line, and the Related Work never mentions ReasoningBank at all - an omission of prior work the authors were literally given.
strongest_objection: The study's own power analysis defeats its own pre-registered decision rules. Measurement states plainly that it 'can adjudicate effects of roughly 3 points and larger under the swapped bank and cannot resolve smaller ones' - yet the rules that decide what the paper concludes all turn on smaller quantities: baseline-1/P8 declare memory dropout unnecessary if reduced-k comes 'within 1.5 points' of it; baseline-2 declares 'just optimize memory-free' if p=1 ties p=0.5 within 2 points; P2 requires p=0.5 to beat p=1 by >=2 points. Three of these are equivalence claims, and none is backed by an equivalence procedure (TOST) powered at the stated margin - failing to reject a 1.5-point difference at MDE~3 is guaranteed, not informative. The realistic outcome is therefore that E2 returns a top-k effect that is neither clearly smaller nor clearly equal to the dropout effect, and P8 - the arm the authors themselves call the most likely way the method dies and one of only two confirmatory tests - cannot be decided in either direction. Compounding this, D_swap as designed is not identified as co-adaptation: instructions are optimized only on split A, so acc(B_A) - acc(B_B) confounds instruction-to-bank co-adaptation with a plain bank main effect (B_B may simply be the weaker distillation). The single hand-written instruction evaluated across three banks is a one-observation, zero-variance handle on that main effect and cannot carry the identification of the paper's primary diagnostic. And because B_A and B_B are distilled from disjoint i.i.d. splits of the same HotpotQA distribution, the swap is an exchangeable resample rather than the incremental self-editing turnover the motivation describes; the most likely Stage-1 outcome is D_swap < 3 points, the gate fires, and the paper is a bounded null on one task with one 7B model.
what_would_fix_it: (1) Counterbalance the swap: optimize at p=0 on split B as well and evaluate crossed (A-instructions on B_A/B_B and B-instructions on B_B/B_A), reporting the instruction x bank interaction rather than a one-directional difference. The re-optimization baseline already produces 3 B-optimized instructions; evaluating them on B_A costs 2,400 episodes and converts D_swap from a confounded difference into an identified interaction. Fund it by dropping E4, whose n=21 pooled Spearman is confounded by condition (p=0 instructions have high verbatim overlap and high D_swap by construction, so rho>=0.5 is a design artifact, not evidence of mechanism). (2) Re-specify every 'within X points' rule as a TOST with an equivalence margin the design is actually powered for, and raise the margins to >=3 points or raise n/seeds until 1.5 points is resolvable; as written the paper cannot conclude what its own contingency table says it will conclude. (3) Add a same-size random/shuffled-content bank at deployment, so 'swapped' is separated from 'any bank other than the one I saw'. (4) Actually run the dated preprint search now, including ReasoningBank and 'prompt optimization validation overfitting / distribution shift', and report it - the promise to search 'before submission' is not reviewable.
missing_baseline: The counterbalanced (bidirectional) swap: instructions optimized on bank B_B evaluated on B_A. The plan optimizes on split A only and evaluates on {B_A, B_B, none}, so the primary diagnostic D_swap cannot be separated from a bank-quality main effect except via a single deterministic hand-written instruction. Secondary omission: a random-content / shuffled bank of matched size at deployment, which would distinguish 'the instruction is bound to *this* bank' from 'the instruction degrades under *any* unfamiliar bank' - the neutral-block arm tests optimization-time perturbation, not deployment-time bank identity, and does not cover this.
preprint_collision: The check is not thin - it is empty, and the authors say so: 'Every web-search call in this session returned a hard server-side tool use limit exceeded error; not one query returned data', with 'zero verified evidence' and novelty 'unverified'. Under the standard that an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness rather than a neutral, this is the single largest deduction, and it is the second consecutive draft in which the search failed. The honesty is creditable and the comparative restructuring is a sensible hedge, but a reviewer cannot grade a search that will happen 'before submission'. I cannot name a specific colliding arXiv preprint under the no-search constraint of this review either, so I score novelty on what is established rather than on what might exist - and what is established is that the intervention is conceded as non-novel (FiD-style document dropping, randomized retrieved-context masking) and the framing rests on an unchecked belief. The planned query list is also incomplete in ways the authors could fix from the materials in hand: it omits 'ReasoningBank' (named in the track brief they were given), 'prompt optimizer overfitting validation set', 'DSPy distribution shift robustness', and 'in-context demonstration dropout', which are the searches most likely to surface a collision with P1.
